A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hidden Profile research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, mathematical content, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments across six LLMs and nine tasks, a 96-participant human study, and prompting experiments in Sections 4–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original human and LLM experiments, task-generation validation outcomes, expanded benchmark evaluations, and additional prompting results in Appendix A.2.

M1.justification: V2 Section 5.1.2 adds an automatic benchmark-construction procedure: GPT-4.1 generates candidates, evaluates their Full and Hidden Profile solvability, and filters them using accuracy thresholds. V1 constructs and adapts tasks without this generation-and-selection pipeline. The underlying multi-agent discussion framework remains broadly similar.

E1.justification: Coverage changes from three evacuation scenarios plus six adapted tasks to three crafted, five adapted, and 57 generated tasks. V2 includes healthcare, organizational planning, and cultural-preservation scenarios. Lewis 2022, evaluated in v1 Figure 3, is absent from v2's five-task adaptation list.

E2.justification: The cross-model comparison changes substantially between v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 4. GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 remain, while o4-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Llama-3.3, and Qwen-2.5VL disappear. V2 evaluates GPT-4.1 Mini/Nano, GPT-5 variants, Gemini-2.5, Qwen3, and Llama-4 systems.

E3.justification: V2 introduces paired pre-discussion validation trials with Full Profile accuracy at least 80% and Hidden Profile accuracy at most 20%, plus model-size and reasoning-budget comparisons such as GPT-5 Minimal versus Medium Reasoning. Existing task inputs also change: Table 1's mudslide blocks the driveway in v1 but walking trails in v2, limiting direct comparison of the revised evacuation results.

E4.justification: The five cooperation–contradiction interventions are retained, while v2 adds zero-shot chain-of-thought and explicit information-asymmetry tests in Table A2. Section 4.3.1 also extends the conversation analysis with early-consensus timing for LLMs and human discussion-length information.

E5.justification: The cross-model benchmark changes from 30 Hidden and 50 Complete Profile repetitions in v1 Section 5.2 to 10 per condition in v2 Section 5.2. Fisher tests and mean ± s.e.m. reporting remain, but uncertainty presentation changes: v2's aggregate model chart includes error bars, whereas Table A1 omits the prompting uncertainty previously shown in v1 Figure 4.

E6.justification: Under the respective evacuation setups, GPT-4.1 Hidden Profile post-discussion accuracy is 0.200 in v1 and 0.233 in v2; Full Profile pre-discussion accuracy is 0.433 and 0.733. These are revised-setting results, not established same-setting gains. V1's steadily increasing tone-series accuracy is replaced by nonmonotonic results in Table A1, including 0.017 for Conflictual. V2 additionally reports 57/200 successful task validations and extensive new aggregate benchmark results.

T1.justification: The central information-distribution model, Hidden Profile condition, and average/majority aggregation rules are retained in condensed form. V2 Figure 4 introduces an explicit mathematical criterion for strong collective reasoning: Yfull > 0.8 and Ypost − Ypre > 0.4 × (Yfull − Ypre). No new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: V2's abstract and contributions center on a scalable 65-task benchmark, persistent failures under prompting changes, and findings that model scale and reasoning enhancements do not reliably predict collective reasoning. V1's prominent social-desirability and cooperation–contradiction claims recede. The central claim that distributed-information groups underperform Full Profile individuals remains.

C2.justification: V1 explains North Hill failures through social desirability and interprets contradiction as improving critical reasoning at a consensus cost. V2 removes that specific social-desirability explanation and emphasizes premature consensus, limited prompting effectiveness, and collective capability being distinct from model scale or individual reasoning. These substantially revise the explanatory narrative.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix A.1 supplies a detailed generation prompt, output schema, design checks, and worked evacuation example, alongside revised discussion and voting templates. Conversely, v1's API-provider information, hardware specification, approximately ten-hour runtime, and default-hyperparameter disclosure are removed. These are substantial documentation changes, not evidence that every underlying implementation setting changed.

R1.justification: The Hidden Profile and social-psychology foundations remain. V2 adds Lu et al.'s meta-analysis, Stasser and Titus (1987), Wei et al. (2022), and newer multi-agent framework/scaling references. It removes Lewis et al. (2022) and much of v1's exploration–exploitation and human–AI future-work bibliography, updating the supporting literature without replacing the central intellectual grounding.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion around HiddenBench. The framework/setup/experiments sequence becomes a formalization followed by Study 1 and Study 2; mathematical exposition is condensed, terminology changes from Complete to Full Profile, and the appendix is extensively reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 substantially redesigns Figure 2 and replaces v1's task-by-model heatmaps with an aggregate horizontal-bar comparison containing performance-gap columns. It adds a generation-pipeline diagram, combines the earlier tone instructions and plotted experiment into Appendix Table A1, and adds Table A2. The document template and appendix presentation also change extensively.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the documented generation-and-screening procedure: v2 explicitly checks generated tasks for high Full Profile and low Hidden Profile accuracy, strengthening the separation of individual task difficulty from distributed-information failure. Complete generation instructions and broader evaluations make the benchmark substantially more reusable and diagnostically useful. These gains outweigh lost per-task and implementation detail. A material weakness remains: Section 4.3.2 dismisses informing agents about asymmetry despite Table A2 reporting 0.367 accuracy versus the default 0.233, without uncertainty supporting that dismissal.
